title: Book 3, Chapter 9 — Fourth and Fifth Years of the War—Revolt of Mitylene
paragraphs: The next summer, just as the corn was ripening, the Peloponnesians and their allies invaded Attica under Archidamus, son of Zeuxidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians. They settled down and ravaged the land. As usual the Athenian horse attacked them wherever it was practicable, and kept the mass of the light troops from advancing out of their camp to lay waste the parts near the city. The invaders stayed as long as the provisions they had brought allowed, then retired and dispersed to their several cities.

Immediately after the Peloponnesians invaded, all of Lesbos except Methymna revolted from the Athenians. The Lesbians had wished to revolt even before the war, but the Lacedaemonians would not receive them. Even now that they did revolt, they were forced to do it sooner than they had intended. They were still waiting for the moles at their harbors, the ships and the walls they had under construction to be finished, and for the archers, corn and other supplies they were bringing in from the Pontus. Meanwhile the Tenedians, with whom they were at enmity, the Methymnians, and some factious persons in Mitylene itself who were proxeni of Athens, informed the Athenians. They said that the Mitylenians were forcing the island into a union under their own sovereignty, and that all their busy preparations were being concerted with the Boeotians, their kindred, and with the Lacedaemonians, with a view to revolt. Unless they were stopped at once, Athens would lose Lesbos.

The Athenians, however, were distressed by the plague and by the war that had recently broken out and was now raging. They thought it a serious matter to add Lesbos, with its fleet and untouched resources, to the list of their enemies. At first they would not believe the charge, giving too much weight to their wish that it might not be true. But they sent an embassy, and when it failed to persuade the Mitylenians to give up the union and the preparations complained of, they became alarmed and resolved to strike the first blow. So they suddenly sent off forty ships, which had been made ready to sail round Peloponnese, under Cleippides, son of Deinias, and two others. They had been told of a festival of the Malean Apollo outside the town, which the whole people of Mitylene keep, and they hoped that if they made haste they could take the Mitylenians by surprise. If this plan succeeded, well and good. If not, the commanders were to order the Mitylenians to hand over their ships and pull down their walls, and if the Mitylenians did not obey, to declare war. The ships set out. The ten galleys that the Mitylenians had with the fleet as their contingent under the terms of the alliance were detained by the Athenians, and their crews placed in custody. The Mitylenians, however, were informed of the expedition by a man who crossed from Athens to Euboea, went overland to Geraestus, and sailed from there on a merchantman he found on the point of putting to sea. He reached Mitylene on the third day after leaving Athens. So the Mitylenians did not go out to the temple at Malea, and they also barricaded the half-finished parts of their walls and harbors and kept guard around them.

The Athenians sailed in not long afterward and saw how things stood. The generals delivered their orders, and when the Mitylenians refused to obey, they began hostilities. The Mitylenians were thus forced into war without notice and unprepared. At first they sailed out with their fleet and made some show of fighting, a little in front of the harbor. But they were driven back by the Athenian ships, and at once offered to treat with the commanders, wishing if possible to get the ships away for the present on any tolerable terms. The Athenian commanders accepted, since they themselves feared they might not be able to cope with the whole of Lesbos. An armistice was concluded, and the Mitylenians sent to Athens one of the informers, who already repented of what he had done, and others with him, to try to persuade the Athenians that their intentions were innocent and to get the fleet recalled. In the meantime they had no great hope of a favorable answer from Athens, so they also sent off a galley with envoys to Lacedaemon, unobserved by the Athenian fleet, which was anchored at Malea to the north of the town.

These envoys reached Lacedaemon after a difficult journey across the open sea, and were negotiating for help to be sent to them. Meanwhile the ambassadors from Athens returned having accomplished nothing, and the Mitylenians and the rest of Lesbos at once began hostilities. The exception was the Methymnians, who came to the aid of the Athenians with the Imbrians, the Lemnians and a few of the other allies. The Mitylenians made a sortie with all their forces against the Athenian camp, and a battle followed in which they gained some slight advantage. They retired nonetheless, not having enough confidence in themselves to spend the night on the field. After this they kept quiet. They wished to wait for reinforcements from Peloponnese before making a second venture, and they were encouraged by the arrival of Meleas, a Laconian, and Hermaeondas, a Theban. These two had been sent off before the insurrection but had been unable to reach Lesbos before the Athenian expedition. They now stole in on a galley after the battle, and advised the Mitylenians to send another galley and envoys back with them, which the Mitylenians did.

Meanwhile the Athenians were greatly encouraged by the inaction of the Mitylenians. They summoned allies to their aid, who came in all the quicker because they saw so little vigor from the Lesbians. The Athenians brought their ships round to a new station south of the town, fortified two camps, one on each side of the city, and set up a blockade of both harbors. The sea was thus closed against the Mitylenians. They did, however, command the whole country, together with the rest of the Lesbians who had now joined them. The Athenians held only a limited area around their camps, and used Malea more as the station for their ships and as their market.

While the war went on in this way at Mitylene, the Athenians also sent thirty ships to Peloponnese about the same time in this summer, under Asopius, son of Phormio. The Acarnanians had insisted that the commander sent should be some son or relative of Phormio. As the ships coasted along they ravaged the seaboard of Laconia. Asopius then sent most of the fleet home and himself went on with twelve vessels to Naupactus. There he raised the whole Acarnanian population and made an expedition against Oeniadae, the fleet sailing along the Achelous while the army laid waste the country. The inhabitants showed no signs of submitting, so he dismissed the land forces and sailed to Leucas himself. He made a descent upon Nericus, and during his retreat he was cut off and killed, with most of his troops, by the people of those parts, helped by some coastguards. After this the Athenians sailed away, recovering their dead from the Leucadians under truce.

Meanwhile the envoys sent out by the Mitylenians in the first ship were told by the Lacedaemonians to come to Olympia, so that the rest of the allies could hear them and decide on their request. They journeyed there. It was the Olympiad in which the Rhodian Dorieus won his second victory. The envoys were introduced to make their speech after the festival, and spoke as follows:

“Lacedaemonians and allies, the rule that holds among the Hellenes is well known to us. When men revolt in war and abandon their former confederacy, those who receive them think well of them only so far as they are useful. Otherwise they think them worse men, since they regard them as traitors to their former friends. This is not an unfair judgment when the rebels and the power they leave are at one in policy and sympathy, are evenly matched in resources and power, and when the rebellion has no reasonable ground. But this was not so with us and the Athenians. No one need think the worse of us for revolting from them in a time of danger, when they had honored us in time of peace.

“Justice and honesty will be the first topics of our speech, especially as we are asking for an alliance. We know that there can never be any solid friendship between individuals, nor any union between communities worth the name, unless the parties are persuaded of each other’s honesty and are generally congenial to one another, since difference in feeling gives rise also to difference in conduct. Our alliance with the Athenians began when you withdrew from the Median War and they remained to finish the business. But we did not become allies of the Athenians for the subjugation of the Hellenes. We became allies of the Hellenes for their liberation from the Mede. As long as the Athenians led us fairly we followed them loyally. But when we saw them relax their hostility to the Mede in order to try to bring the allies into subjection, our apprehensions began. The allies could not unite to defend themselves, because there were so many confederates with votes, and all were enslaved except ourselves and the Chians, who went on sending our contingents as independent and nominally free. Trust in Athens as a leader, however, we could no longer feel, judging by the examples already given. It was unlikely that she would reduce our fellow confederates and not do the same to us who were left, if ever she had the power.

“Had we all remained independent, we could have trusted them more not to attempt any change. But most of the allies were their subjects and only we were treated as equals, and they would naturally resent this one case of independence beside the submission of the rest. They would resent it all the more because they grew stronger daily and we grew poorer. Now the only sure basis of an alliance is that each side fears the other equally. Whoever would like to encroach is then held back by the thought that the odds will not be in his favor. Again, if we were left independent, it was only because they believed they could reach empire more surely by fair speeches and policy than by force. We served them as evidence: powers with votes, like themselves, would surely not join their expeditions against their will unless the party attacked were in the wrong. The same system also let them lead the stronger states against the weaker first, and so leave the stronger to the last, stripped of their natural allies and less able to resist. Had they begun with us, while every state still controlled its own resources and there was a center to rally round, subjugation would have proved harder. Our navy, besides, gave them some apprehension: it might join you or some other power and become dangerous to Athens. The court we paid to their commons and to its leaders of the moment also helped us keep our independence. Even so, judging by what we had seen of their conduct toward the rest, we did not expect to keep it much longer, had this war not broken out.

“How then could we put our trust in such friendship or freedom as we had here? We accepted each other against our inclination. Fear made them court us in war, and us them in peace. Sympathy, the ordinary basis of confidence, was replaced by terror, and fear had more share than friendship in keeping us in the alliance. The first party to be encouraged by the hope of impunity was certain to break faith with the other. So to condemn us for being the first to break off, because they delay the blow that we dread, instead of our delaying to learn for certain whether it will be dealt or not, is to take a false view of the case. For if we were as able as they are to meet their plots and imitate their delay, we should be their equals and under no necessity of being their subjects. But since the liberty of offense is always theirs, the liberty of defense ought clearly to be ours.

“Such, Lacedaemonians and allies, are the grounds and the reasons of our revolt. They are clear enough to convince our hearers that we acted fairly, and serious enough to alarm us and drive us to look for some means of safety. We wished to do this long ago, when we sent to you about it while the peace still lasted, but you stopped us by refusing to receive us. Now that the Boeotians have invited us, we have answered the call at once. We decided on a twofold revolt, from the Hellenes and from the Athenians: we did not wish to help the Athenians harm the Hellenes, but to join in the Hellenes’ liberation, and we did not wish to let the Athenians destroy us in the end, but to act against them in time. Our revolt, however, has come prematurely and without preparation — which makes it all the more your duty to receive us into alliance and send us speedy relief, to show that you support your friends and at the same time injure your enemies. You have an opportunity such as you never had before. Disease and expense have worn the Athenians down. Their ships are either cruising round your coasts or blockading us, and they are not likely to have any to spare if you invade them a second time this summer by sea and land. They will either offer your vessels no resistance, or withdraw from both our shores. Nor should you think that you would be running risks for a country that is not yours. Lesbos may seem far off, but when help is wanted she will be found near enough. The war will not be decided in Attica, as some imagine, but in the countries that support Attica. The Athenian revenue comes from the allies, and it will grow larger still if they reduce us. No other state will revolt, our resources will be added to theirs, and we shall be treated worse than those who were enslaved before. But if you support us frankly, you will gain a state with a large navy, which is your great want. You will smooth the way to the overthrow of the Athenians by depriving them of their allies, who will be greatly encouraged to come over. And you will clear yourselves of the charge that you do not support insurrection. In short, only show yourselves as liberators, and you may count on having the advantage in the war.

“Respect, therefore, the hopes the Hellenes place in you, and Olympian Zeus, in whose temple we stand as very suppliants. Become the allies and defenders of the Mitylenians, and do not sacrifice us, who put our lives at hazard in a cause from which general good will result to all if we succeed, and still more general harm if we fail because you refuse to help us. But be the men that the Hellenes think you, and our fears desire.”

Such were the words of the Mitylenians. After hearing them out, the Lacedaemonians and confederates granted what they urged and took the Lesbians into alliance. They decided in favor of invading Attica, and told the allies present to march as quickly as possible to the Isthmus with two-thirds of their forces. The Lacedaemonians arrived there first themselves, and got ready hauling machines to carry their ships across from Corinth to the sea on the side of Athens, so as to attack by sea and land at once. However, the rest of the confederates did not imitate their zeal. They came in slowly, being engaged in harvesting their corn and sick of making expeditions.

Meanwhile the Athenians were aware that the enemy’s preparations were due to his conviction of their weakness. They wished to show him that he was mistaken, and that without moving the Lesbian fleet they were able to repel with ease the threat from Peloponnese. So they manned a hundred ships, embarking the citizens of Athens except the knights and Pentacosiomedimni, and the resident aliens. They put out to the Isthmus, displayed their power, and made descents on Peloponnese wherever they pleased. So signal a disappointment made the Lacedaemonians think that the Lesbians had not spoken the truth. They were also embarrassed by the non-appearance of the confederates and by the news that the thirty ships round Peloponnese were ravaging the lands near Sparta, and so they went back home. Afterward, however, they got ready a fleet to send to Lesbos. They ordered a total of forty ships from the different cities in the league, and appointed Alcidas to command the expedition as high admiral. Meanwhile the Athenians in the hundred ships saw the Lacedaemonians go home, and went home likewise.

When this fleet was at sea, Athens had almost the largest number of first-rate ships in commission that she ever had at one time. But she had as many, or even more, when the war began. Then a hundred guarded Attica, Euboea and Salamis, and another hundred were cruising round Peloponnese, besides those employed at Potidæa and elsewhere. In all, two hundred and fifty vessels were on active service in a single summer. This, together with Potidæa, did most to exhaust her revenues. A force of heavy infantry blockaded Potidæa, each man drawing two drachmae a day, one for himself and one for his servant. At first there were three thousand of them, and this number was kept up to the end of the siege, besides sixteen hundred with Phormio who left before it was over. The ships were all paid at the same rate. In this way her money was wasted at first, and this was the largest number of ships she ever manned.

About the same time that the Lacedaemonians were at the Isthmus, the Mitylenians marched by land with their mercenaries against Methymna, which they thought to gain by treachery. They assaulted the town but did not meet with the success they anticipated. They withdrew to Antissa, Pyrrha and Eresus, took measures to make these towns more secure and strengthened their walls, and hastily returned home. After their departure the Methymnians marched against Antissa, but the Antissians and their mercenaries defeated them in a sortie, and they retreated in haste after losing many of their number. Word of this reached Athens. The Athenians learned that the Mitylenians were masters of the country and that their own soldiers were unable to hold them in check. So about the beginning of autumn they sent out Paches, son of Epicurus, to take command, with a thousand Athenian heavy infantry, who worked their own passage. They arrived at Mitylene and built a single wall all round it, with forts erected at some of the strongest points. Mitylene was thus strictly blockaded on both sides, by land and by sea, and winter was now drawing near.

The Athenians needed money for the siege. Although they had for the first time raised a contribution of two hundred talents from their own citizens, they now sent out twelve ships under Lysicles and four others to collect subsidies from their allies. Lysicles cruised to various places and laid them under contribution. Then he went inland from Myus, in Caria, across the plain of the Meander, as far as the hill of Sandius. There the Carians and the people of Anaia attacked him, and he was slain with many of his soldiers.

The same winter the Plataeans, still besieged by the Peloponnesians and Boeotians, were distressed because their provisions had failed. They saw no hope of relief from Athens and no other means of safety. So they planned with the Athenians besieged alongside them to escape, if possible, by forcing a way over the enemy’s walls. The attempt was suggested by Theaenetus, son of Tolmides, a soothsayer, and Eupompides, son of Daimachus, one of their generals. At first all were to join, but afterward half hung back, thinking the risk great. About two hundred and twenty, however, volunteered and kept to the attempt, which was carried out in the following way. They made ladders to match the height of the enemy’s wall, and they measured the wall by its layers of bricks, because the side facing them was not thoroughly whitewashed. Many people counted the layers at the same time. Some might get the figure wrong, but most would hit on it, particularly since they counted again and again and were not far from the wall, and could see it well enough for their purpose. They got the length needed for the ladders by calculating from the breadth of a brick.

This is how the wall of the Peloponnesians was built. It was made of two lines drawn round the place, about sixteen feet apart: one faced the Plataeans, the other faced any attack from outside coming from Athens. The sixteen feet between them were filled with huts divided among the soldiers on guard. These were built in one block, so that the whole looked like a single thick wall with battlements on both sides. At every tenth battlement stood a large tower, as broad as the wall, extending from its inner face to its outer, so that the only way past was through the middle. On stormy and wet nights, therefore, the soldiers left the battlements and kept guard from the towers, which were close together and roofed over.

Such was the structure of the wall by which the Plataeans were blockaded. When their preparations were completed, they waited for a stormy night of wind and rain and without any moon, and then set out, guided by the authors of the enterprise. They first crossed the ditch that ran round the town, and next reached the enemy’s wall unperceived by the sentinels, who did not see them in the darkness or hear them, since the wind drowned the noise of their approach with its roar. Besides this, they kept a good way off from each other, so that the clash of their weapons would not betray them. They were also lightly equipped, and had only the left foot shod, to keep them from slipping in the mire. They came up to the battlements at one of the intermediate spaces, where they knew them to be unguarded. Those who carried the ladders went first and planted them. Next twelve light-armed soldiers, with only a dagger and a breastplate, mounted, led by Ammias, son of Coroebus, who was the first on the wall. His followers got up after him and went six to each of the towers. After these came another party of light troops armed with spears. Their shields were carried by men behind them, so that they could advance more easily, and these were to hand them over when they found themselves in the presence of the enemy. After a good many had mounted, the sentinels in the towers discovered them, from the noise made by a tile that one of the Plataeans knocked down as he took hold of the battlements. The alarm was given at once, and the troops rushed to the wall, not knowing the nature of the danger, owing to the dark night and stormy weather. The Plataeans in the town had also chosen that moment to make a sortie against the wall of the Peloponnesians on the side opposite to that where their men were getting over, in order to divert the attention of the besiegers. So the Peloponnesians remained distracted at their several posts, none of them venturing to stir from his own station to give help, and at a loss to guess what was going on. Meanwhile the three hundred set aside for service in emergencies went outside the wall in the direction of the alarm. Fire-signals of an attack were also raised toward Thebes. But the Plataeans in the town at once displayed a number of others, prepared beforehand for this very purpose, in order to make the enemy’s signals unintelligible, and to prevent his friends from getting a true idea of what was passing and coming to his aid before the comrades who had gone out had made good their escape and were in safety.

Meanwhile the first of the scaling party to get up had taken both the towers and put the sentinels to the sword. They took positions inside to stop anyone coming through against them. They set ladders against the towers from the wall and sent several men up, and from the top and the foot of the towers these men used missiles to hold back every enemy who approached. The main body put a number of ladders against the wall, knocked down the battlements, and crossed between the towers. Each man, once over, took his stand at the edge of the ditch and shot arrows and darts at anyone coming along the wall to block his comrades’ passage. When all were across, the men on the towers came down, the last of them with difficulty, and went to the ditch, just as the three hundred arrived carrying torches. The Plataeans stood on the edge of the ditch in the dark and could see their opponents well. They shot arrows and darts at their unprotected parts, while the torches made it hard for the Peloponnesians to see them in the obscurity. And so even the last of them got over the ditch, though only with effort and difficulty. Ice had formed in it, too weak to walk on, of the watery kind that generally comes with a wind more east than north. The snow that this wind had brought in the night had raised the water in the ditch, so that they could scarcely breast it as they crossed. Still, it was mainly the violence of the storm that made their escape possible at all.

From the ditch the Plataeans went all together along the road to Thebes, keeping the chapel of the hero Androcrates on their right. They reckoned that the last road the Peloponnesians would suspect them of taking was the one toward their enemies’ country. Indeed they could see the Peloponnesians chasing them with torches along the Athens road, toward Cithaeron and Druoskephalai, or Oakheads. When they had gone rather more than half a mile on the road to Thebes, the Plataeans turned off onto the road to the mountain, to Erythrae and Hysiae. They reached the hills and escaped to Athens, two hundred and twelve men in all. Some of their number had turned back into the town before crossing the wall, and one archer had been taken prisoner at the outer ditch. Meanwhile the Peloponnesians gave up the pursuit and returned to their posts. The Plataeans in the town knew nothing of what had happened. Those who had turned back told them that not a man had escaped, and as soon as it was day they sent out a herald to arrange a truce for the recovery of the dead. Then they learned the truth and desisted. In this way the Plataean party got over and were saved.

Toward the end of the same winter, Salaethus, a Lacedaemonian, was sent in a galley from Lacedaemon to Mitylene. He sailed to Pyrrha and went on overland, following the bed of a torrent at a point where the line of circumvallation could be crossed. In this way he entered Mitylene unperceived. He told the magistrates that Attica would certainly be invaded and that the forty ships meant to relieve them would arrive, and that he had been sent ahead to announce this and to take charge of matters generally. The Mitylenians took courage at this and gave up the idea of treating with the Athenians. And now this winter ended, and with it the fourth year of the war of which Thucydides was the historian.

The next summer the Peloponnesians sent the forty-two ships to Mitylene under Alcidas, their high admiral. They and their allies themselves invaded Attica, intending to distract the Athenians with a double movement, so that it would be harder for them to act against the fleet sailing to Mitylene. The commander of this invasion was Cleomenes, who held the place of King Pausanias, son of Pleistoanax, his nephew, who was still a minor. The invaders were not content with laying waste whatever had grown up again in the districts they had devastated before. They now extended their ravages to lands they had passed over in earlier incursions, so that the Athenians felt this invasion more severely than any except the second. The enemy stayed on and on until they had overrun most of the country, expecting to hear from Lesbos that their fleet had achieved something, for they thought it must by now have crossed. However, none of the expected results came, and their provisions began to run short. So they retreated and dispersed to their several cities.

In the meantime the Mitylenians found their provisions failing, while the fleet from Peloponnese was loitering on the way instead of appearing at Mitylene. They were compelled to come to terms with the Athenians, and it happened in this manner. Salaethus himself no longer expected the fleet to arrive, and he now gave the commons heavy armor, which they had not possessed before, intending to make a sortie against the Athenians. But as soon as the commons found themselves in possession of arms, they refused to obey their officers any longer. They formed in knots and told the authorities to bring the provisions out in public and divide them among all, or else they would themselves come to terms with the Athenians and hand over the city.

The government knew that it could not prevent this, and that it would be in danger if it were left out of the capitulation. So it publicly agreed with Paches and the army to surrender Mitylene at discretion and to admit the troops into the town. The agreement was that the Mitylenians should be allowed to send an embassy to Athens to plead their cause, and that Paches should not imprison, enslave or put to death any of the citizens until it returned. Such were the terms of the capitulation. Even so, the chief authors of the negotiation with Lacedaemon were so overcome by terror when the army entered that they went and seated themselves by the altars. Paches raised them up from there with a promise that he would do them no wrong, and lodged them in Tenedos until he should learn the pleasure of the Athenians concerning them. Paches also sent some galleys and seized Antissa, and took such other military measures as he thought advisable.

Meanwhile the Peloponnesians in the forty ships, who ought to have made all haste to relieve Mitylene, lost time sailing around Peloponnese itself, and went leisurely on the rest of the voyage. They reached Delos without being seen by the Athenians at Athens, and from there arrived at Icarus and Myconus, where they first heard of the fall of Mitylene. Wishing to know the truth, they put into Embatum, in the Erythraeid, about seven days after the capture of the town. There they learned the truth and began to consider what to do. Teutiaplus, an Elean, addressed them as follows:

“Alcidas and Peloponnesians, you who share with me the command of this armament, my advice is to sail to Mitylene just as we are, before anyone has heard of us. We may expect to find the Athenians as much off their guard as men generally are when they have just taken a city. This will certainly be so by sea, where they have no idea that any enemy will attack them and where, as it happens, our strength mainly lies. Even their land forces are probably scattered about the houses in the carelessness of victory. So if we fell upon them suddenly and in the night, I have hopes that we shall become masters of the place, with the help of the well-wishers we may have left inside the town. Let us not shrink from the risk. Let us remember that this is just the occasion for one of the baseless panics common in war, and that a successful general is one who can guard against such panics in his own case and can detect the moment when an attack will find the enemy at this disadvantage.”

Teutiaplus did not move Alcidas. Some of the Ionian exiles and the Lesbians who were with the expedition then pressed him with another plan, since this one seemed too dangerous: to seize one of the Ionian cities, or the Aeolic town of Cyme, and use it as a base to bring about the revolt of Ionia. This was by no means a hopeless enterprise, because their coming would be welcome everywhere. By this move they would aim to deprive Athens of her chief source of revenue, and also to burden her with expense should she choose to blockade them. They would probably also persuade Pissuthnes to join them in the war. Alcidas, however, received this proposal as badly as the other. He had come too late for Mitylene, and he was eager to be back in Peloponnese as soon as possible.

Accordingly he put out from Embatum and proceeded along the shore. Touching at the Teian town of Myonnesus, he butchered there most of the prisoners he had taken on the voyage. When he came to anchor at Ephesus, envoys came to him from the Samians at Anaia. They told him that he was not going the right way to free Hellas when he massacred men who had never raised a hand against him, men who were not his enemies but allies of Athens against their will. If he did not stop, they said, he would turn many more friends into enemies than enemies into friends. Alcidas agreed, and let go all the Chians still in his hands and some of the others he had taken. The inhabitants, instead of fleeing at the sight of his vessels, had rather come up to them, taking them for Athenian, for they had no expectation at all that Peloponnesian ships would venture over to Ionia while the Athenians commanded the sea.

From Ephesus Alcidas set sail in haste and fled. While he was still at anchor off Clarus, the Salaminian and Paralian galleys, which happened to be sailing from Athens, had seen him. Fearing pursuit, he now made across the open sea, fully determined to touch nowhere, if he could help it, until he reached Peloponnese. Meanwhile news of him had come in to Paches from the Erythraeid, and indeed from all quarters. Ionia was unfortified, and great fears were felt that the Peloponnesians, coasting along the shore, might make descents in passing and plunder the towns, even if they did not intend to stay. And now the Paralian and Salaminian, having seen him at Clarus, themselves brought word of it. Paches accordingly gave hot chase and continued the pursuit as far as the isle of Patmos. Then, finding that Alcidas had got too far ahead to be overtaken, he came back again. Meanwhile he thought it fortunate that, since he had not fallen in with them out at sea, he had not overtaken them anywhere that would have forced them to encamp, and so given him the trouble of blockading them.

On his way back along the shore he touched, among other places, at Notium, the port of Colophon. The Colophonians had settled there after Itamenes and the barbarians took the upper town; certain individuals in a party quarrel had called these barbarians in. That capture took place about the time of the second Peloponnesian invasion of Attica. After settling at Notium, however, the refugees again split into factions. One faction brought in Arcadian and barbarian mercenaries from Pissuthnes, entrenched them in a separate quarter, and formed a new community together with those Colophonians of the Median party who joined them from the upper town. Their opponents had gone into exile, and now called in Paches. He invited Hippias, who commanded the Arcadians in the fortified quarter, to a parley, on condition that Hippias would be put back safe and sound in the fortification if they could not agree. But when Hippias came out to him, Paches put him into custody, though not in chains. Then he attacked the fortification suddenly and took it by surprise, and put to the sword the Arcadians and barbarians he found in it. After that he took Hippias into it, as he had promised, and as soon as Hippias was inside, seized him and shot him down. Paches then gave Notium up to the Colophonians who were not of the Median party. Settlers were afterwards sent out from Athens, and the place was colonized according to Athenian laws, once all the Colophonians found in any of the cities had been gathered together.

On reaching Mitylene, Paches reduced Pyrrha and Eresus. He found the Lacedaemonian Salaethus in hiding in the town and sent him to Athens, along with the Mitylenians he had placed in Tenedos and anyone else he thought implicated in the revolt. He also sent back most of his forces. With the rest he stayed behind to settle Mitylene and the rest of Lesbos as he thought best.

When the prisoners arrived with Salaethus, the Athenians at once put him to death, although he offered, among other things, to procure the withdrawal of the Peloponnesians from Plataea, which was still under siege. Then they deliberated about what to do with the others. In the fury of the moment they determined to put to death not only the prisoners at Athens but the whole adult male population of Mitylene, and to make slaves of the women and children. It was remarked that Mitylene had revolted without having been, like the rest, subjected to the empire. What above all swelled the wrath of the Athenians was that the Peloponnesian fleet had ventured over to Ionia to support her, a fact which was held to argue a long-meditated rebellion. They accordingly sent a galley to communicate the decree to Paches, commanding him to lose no time in dispatching the Mitylenians. The next day brought repentance, and reflection on the horrid cruelty of a decree which condemned a whole city to the fate merited only by the guilty. The Mitylenian ambassadors at Athens and their Athenian supporters soon perceived this, and moved the authorities to put the question to the vote again. The authorities the more easily consented, since they themselves plainly saw that most of the citizens wished someone to give them an opportunity to reconsider the matter. An assembly was therefore called at once. After much expression of opinion on both sides, Cleon, son of Cleaenetus, came forward again. He was the same man who had carried the former motion to put the Mitylenians to death, the most violent man at Athens, and at that time by far the most powerful with the commons. He spoke as follows:

“I have often been convinced before now that a democracy cannot govern an empire, and never more so than by your present change of mind about Mitylene. You know no fears or plots in your daily dealings with each other, and you feel just the same toward your allies. It never occurs to you that when you listen to their appeals, or give way to your own compassion, you make mistakes that are full of danger to yourselves and win you no thanks from your allies for your weakness. You forget completely that your empire is a despotism and your subjects disaffected conspirators. They obey you not because of your suicidal concessions, but because of the superiority your own strength gives you, not because of any loyalty of theirs. What alarms me most is the constant change of measures with which we seem to be threatened, and our apparent ignorance that bad laws which are never changed are better for a city than good laws that have no authority. Unlearned loyalty is more serviceable than quick-witted insubordination, and ordinary men usually manage public affairs better than their more gifted fellows. The gifted are always wanting to appear wiser than the laws and to overrule every proposal put forward, believing that they could show their wit in no more important matter; and by such behavior they too often ruin their country. Those who distrust their own cleverness are content to be less learned than the laws and less able to find fault with the speech of a good speaker. They act as fair judges, not as rival athletes, and so they generally conduct affairs successfully. These are the men we ought to imitate, rather than being led on by cleverness and intellectual rivalry to advise your people against our real opinions.

“For myself, I hold to my former opinion. I am amazed at those who have proposed to reopen the case of the Mitylenians, because they cause a delay that favors only the guilty: the injured party must now go after the offender when the edge of his anger has been blunted. And yet vengeance that follows most closely on the wrong best matches it and most fully requites it. I am amazed too at whoever will rise to maintain the contrary, and pretend to show that the crimes of the Mitylenians benefit us and our misfortunes harm the allies. Plainly such a man must either be so confident in his rhetoric as to venture to prove that a question settled once for all is still undecided, or else be bribed to try to delude us with elaborate sophisms. In such contests the state hands out the rewards to others and keeps the dangers for herself. The blame lies with you, who are foolish enough to set up these contests. You go to hear a speech as you would go to see a spectacle. You take your facts on hearsay. You judge whether a project is practicable by the wit of those who advocate it, and as to the truth about past events, you trust less the fact that you saw than the clever criticisms that you heard. You fall easy victims to new-fangled arguments and refuse to follow received conclusions. You are slaves to every new paradox and despisers of the commonplace. Every man’s first wish is to be able to speak himself; failing that, he wants to rival those who can, by seeming to keep right up with their ideas, applauding each hit almost before it is made, and catching an argument as quickly as he is slow to foresee its consequences. You ask, if I may say so, for something other than the conditions under which we live, and yet you do not even comprehend those conditions adequately. You are truly slaves to the pleasure of the ear, and you resemble the audience of a rhetorician more than the council of a city.

“To keep you from this, I will now show that no single state has ever injured you as much as Mitylene has. I can make allowance for those who revolt because they cannot bear our empire, or because the enemy has forced them to it. But these men held an island with fortifications. They had to fear our enemies only by sea, and there they had their own force of galleys to protect them. They were independent, and you held them in the highest honor. When such men act as these have done, it is not revolt, since revolt implies oppression. It is deliberate and wanton aggression, an attempt to ruin us by siding with our bitterest enemies, and a worse offense than a war undertaken on their own account to gain power. The fate of their neighbors who had already rebelled and been subdued taught them nothing, and their own prosperity could not dissuade them from facing danger. They were blindly confident about the future and full of hopes that went beyond their power though not beyond their ambition. They declared war and chose to prefer might to right, deciding to attack not because of any provocation but because the moment seemed propitious. The truth is that great good fortune, when it comes suddenly and unexpectedly, tends to make a people insolent. In most cases it is safer for mankind to have success that is reasonable than success that is not, and it is easier, one may say, for them to ward off adversity than to preserve prosperity. Our mistake has been to distinguish the Mitylenians as we have done. If they had long ago been treated like the rest, they would never have forgotten themselves so far, for human nature is made arrogant by consideration just as surely as it is awed by firmness. Let them now be punished as their crime requires, and do not, while you condemn the aristocracy, absolve the people. This is certain: all of them attacked you without distinction, although they could have come over to us and by now be again in possession of their city. But no, they thought it safer to throw in their lot with the aristocracy, and so joined their rebellion! Consider therefore. Suppose you inflict the same punishment on the ally who is forced to rebel by the enemy and on the one who rebels by his own free choice. Which of them, think you, will not rebel on the slightest pretext, when the reward of success is freedom and the penalty of failure nothing so very terrible? Meanwhile we shall have to risk our money and our lives against one state after another. If we succeed, we shall receive a ruined town, from which we can no longer draw the revenue on which our strength depends. If we fail, we shall have one more enemy on our hands, and the time that might be spent fighting our existing foes will be spent warring with our own allies.

“Therefore the Mitylenians must be given no hope of the mercy due to human infirmity, whether rhetoric may instill it or money may buy it. Their offense was not involuntary but malicious and deliberate, and mercy is only for those who offend unwillingly. So I persist, now as before, in opposing any reversal of your first decision, and any yielding to the three failings most fatal to empire — pity, sentiment and indulgence. Compassion is owed to those who can feel it in return, not to those who will never pity us back but are our natural and necessary foes. The orators who charm us with sentiment may find other and less important arenas for their talents than this one, where the city pays a heavy penalty for a momentary pleasure while they themselves collect fine acknowledgments for their fine phrases. Indulgence should be shown to those who will be our friends in future, not to men who will remain just what they were and as much our enemies as before. To sum up briefly: if you follow my advice, you will do what is just toward the Mitylenians and at the same time expedient; a different decision will not so much oblige them as pass sentence on yourselves. For if they were right to rebel, you must be wrong to rule. If, however, you are determined to rule, right or wrong, then you must carry out your principle and punish the Mitylenians as your interest requires. Otherwise you must give up your empire and practice honesty without danger. Make up your minds, then, to give them like for like. Do not let the victims who escaped the plot be less sensible of it than the conspirators who hatched it. Think what they would have done had they defeated you, especially since they were the aggressors. It is those who wrong their neighbor without cause who pursue their victim to the death, because of the danger they foresee in letting an enemy live. The object of a wanton wrong is more dangerous, if he escapes, than an enemy who has no such grievance. Do not, therefore, betray yourselves. Call back as nearly as you can the moment of your suffering, and the supreme importance you then attached to their reduction. Pay them back now in their turn, and do not yield to present weakness or forget the peril that once hung over you. Punish them as they deserve, and show your other allies by a striking example that the penalty of rebellion is death. Once they understand that, you will not so often have to neglect your enemies while you are fighting your own confederates.”

Such were the words of Cleon. After him came forward Diodotus, son of Eucrates, who had also spoken most strongly in the previous assembly against putting the Mitylenians to death. He spoke as follows:

“I do not blame those who have reopened the case of the Mitylenians, and I do not approve of the protests we have heard against debating important questions more than once. In my opinion the two things most opposed to good counsel are haste and passion. Haste usually goes hand in hand with folly, and passion with coarseness and narrowness of mind. And as for the claim that speech should not be the exponent of action, whoever makes it must be either senseless or interested. He is senseless if he thinks it possible to deal with the uncertain future through any other medium. He is interested if he wishes to carry a disgraceful measure but doubts that he can speak well in a bad cause, and so hopes to frighten opponents and hearers with well-aimed calumny. More intolerable still is to accuse a speaker of making a display in order to be paid for it. If only ignorance were imputed, an unsuccessful speaker could retire with a reputation for honesty, if not for wisdom. The charge of dishonesty, however, makes him suspect if he succeeds and, if he is defeated, a rogue as well as a fool. The city gains nothing from such a system, since fear robs it of its advisers. Indeed, if our speakers are going to make such assertions, it would be better for the country if they could not speak at all, for then we should make fewer blunders. A good citizen should win not by frightening his opponents but by beating them fairly in argument. A wise city will not over-distinguish its best advisers, but it will not deprive them of their due either; and far from punishing an unlucky counselor, it will not even regard him as disgraced. That way, successful orators would be least tempted to sacrifice their convictions to popularity in hope of still higher honors, and unsuccessful ones would be least tempted to use the same popular arts to win over the multitude.

“This is not our way. Besides, as soon as a man is suspected of giving advice, however good, for corrupt motives, we resent him for a gain that we are not even certain he will receive, and we deprive the city of its certain benefit. So plain good advice has come to be no less suspect than bad. The advocate of the most monstrous measures needs deceit to win the people no more than the best counselor needs to lie to be believed. Because of these refinements the city, and the city alone, can never be served openly and without disguise. Whoever does serve it openly is always suspected of serving himself secretly in return. Still, given the magnitude of the interests involved and the position of affairs, we orators must make it our business to look a little farther than you, who judge offhand. This is the more so because we, your advisers, are responsible and you, our audience, are not. If those who gave the advice and those who took it suffered equally, you would judge more calmly. As it is, whenever the whim of the moment leads you into disaster, you visit it upon the single person of your adviser, and not upon yourselves, his numerous companions in error.

“I have not, however, come forward to oppose or to accuse anyone in the matter of Mitylene. For us, as sensible men, the question before us is not their guilt but our interests. However guilty I prove them, I shall not for that reason advise their death, unless it is expedient. Nor, if they should have claims to indulgence, shall I recommend it, unless it is plainly for the good of the country. I consider that we are deliberating more for the future than for the present. Cleon is very positive about the useful deterrent effects that will follow from making rebellion a capital offense. I weigh the interests of the future quite as much as he does, and I am as positive that the contrary is true. And I ask you not to reject my useful considerations in favor of his specious ones. His speech may attract you by seeming the more just, in your present temper against Mitylene. But we are not in a court of justice; we are in a political assembly, and the question is not justice, but how to make the Mitylenians useful to Athens.

“Communities have, of course, enacted the penalty of death for many offenses far lighter than this one. Yet hope still leads men to venture, and no one has ever yet put himself in peril without the inward conviction that he would succeed in his design. Was there ever a city that rebelled without believing that it had, in itself or in its alliances, resources adequate to the enterprise? All of us, states and individuals alike, are prone to err, and no law will prevent it. Otherwise why would men have exhausted the list of punishments in search of enactments to protect them from evildoers? In early times, probably, the penalties for the greatest offenses were less severe. As they were disregarded, the penalty of death was reached by degrees in most cases, and it too is disregarded in the same way. So either some means of terror more terrible than this must be found, or we must admit that this restraint is useless. As long as poverty gives men the courage of necessity, or plenty fills them with the ambition that belongs to insolence and pride, and the other conditions of life remain each in the thralldom of some fatal and master passion, so long will the impulse never fail to drive men into danger. Hope and cupidity do the widest ruin: hope leads and cupidity follows, the one conceiving the attempt, the other suggesting that it will be easy to succeed. These agents are invisible, yet they are far stronger than the dangers that are seen. Fortune also helps the delusion powerfully. By the unexpected aid she sometimes lends, she tempts men to venture with inferior means. This is especially so with communities, because the stakes they play for are the highest, freedom or empire, and when all are acting together, each man irrationally magnifies his own capacity. In short, it is impossible to stop human nature from doing what it has once set its mind upon, whether by force of law or by any other deterrent force whatever, and only great simplicity can hope to do so.

“We must not, therefore, commit ourselves to a false policy out of belief in the efficacy of the punishment of death, or shut rebels out from the hope of repentance and a prompt atonement for their error. Consider for a moment. As things are, a city that has already revolted and sees that it cannot succeed will come to terms while it is still able to refund our expenses and pay tribute afterwards. In the other case, what city, think you, would not prepare better than cities do now, and hold out to the last against its besiegers, if it makes no difference whether it surrenders late or soon? And how can it fail to harm us to be put to the expense of a siege because surrender is out of the question? If we take the city, we receive a ruined town, from which we can no longer draw the revenue that forms our real strength against the enemy. We must not, then, sit as strict judges of the offenders to our own prejudice. We should look instead at how moderate chastisements may let us benefit in future from the revenue-producing powers of our dependencies, and we must resolve to look for our protection not to legal terrors but to careful administration. At present we do exactly the opposite. When a free community, held in subjection by force, rises and asserts its independence, as is only natural, we fancy ourselves obliged to punish it severely as soon as it is reduced. The right course with freemen, however, is not to chastise them rigorously when they do rise, but to watch them rigorously before they rise, to prevent their ever entertaining the idea, and, once the insurrection is suppressed, to make as few as possible responsible for it.

“Only consider what a blunder you would commit by doing as Cleon recommends. As matters stand, the people is your friend in all the cities. Either it does not revolt along with the oligarchy, or, if forced to, it becomes at once the enemy of the insurgents; so in the war against the hostile city you have the masses on your side. But suppose you butcher the people of Mitylene, who had nothing to do with the revolt and who surrendered the town of their own motion as soon as they got arms. You will first commit the crime of killing your benefactors. Next, you will play directly into the hands of the higher classes. When they induce their cities to rise, they will at once have the people on their side, because you have announced in advance the same punishment for the guilty and the innocent. On the contrary, even if the people were guilty, you ought to seem not to notice it, so as not to alienate the only class still friendly to us. In short, I consider it far more useful for the preservation of our empire to put up voluntarily with injustice than to put to death, however justly, those whom it is our interest to keep alive. As for Cleon’s idea that in punishment the claims of justice and expediency can both be satisfied, the facts do not confirm that such a combination is possible.

“Confess, then, that this is the wisest course. Do not concede too much to pity or to indulgence; I no more than Cleon wish you to be influenced by either motive. Be persuaded by me, on the plain merits of the case before you, to try calmly those Mitylenians whom Paches sent off as guilty, and to leave the rest undisturbed. This is at once best for the future and most terrible to your enemies at the present moment, since good policy against an adversary is stronger than the blind attacks of brute force.”

Such were the words of Diodotus. The two opinions just expressed were the ones that most directly contradicted each other. The Athenians, despite their change of feeling, now came to a division, and the show of hands was almost equal, although the motion of Diodotus carried. A second galley was sent off at once in haste, for fear that the first might reach Lesbos in the meantime and find the city destroyed; the first ship had about a day and a night’s start. The Mitylenian ambassadors supplied the vessel with wine and barley-cakes and made great promises if it arrived in time. That made the men so diligent on the voyage that they ate their barley-cakes, kneaded with oil and wine, as they rowed, and slept only by turns while the others were at the oar. Luckily they met no contrary wind. The first ship made no haste on so horrid an errand, while the second pressed on as described, and the first arrived so little ahead of them that Paches had only just read the decree and was preparing to carry out the sentence when the second put into port and prevented the massacre. The danger of Mitylene had indeed been great.

The other party, whom Paches had sent off as the prime movers in the rebellion, were put to death by the Athenians on Cleon’s motion. They numbered rather more than a thousand. The Athenians also pulled down the walls of the Mitylenians and took over their ships. Afterwards no tribute was imposed on the Lesbians. Instead, all their land except that of the Methymnians was divided into three thousand allotments. Three hundred of these were set apart as sacred to the gods, and the rest were assigned by lot to Athenian shareholders, who were sent out to the island. The Lesbians agreed to pay these men a rent of two minae a year for each allotment, and cultivated the land themselves. The Athenians also took over the towns on the mainland that belonged to the Mitylenians, and these became subject to Athens from then on. Such were the events that took place at Lesbos.
